subject: Copywriting
title: Questions as Headlines
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Questions as Headlines.

hook.text: 'Got Milk?' is two words and a question mark. It became one of the most recognized taglines in history.

buildup.text: Questions activate the brain. You can't read a question without trying to answer it. Engagement is automatic.

discovery.text: Betteridge's Law says any headline ending in a question mark can be answered 'no.' Effective questions defy this.

twist.text: Bad question headlines let readers answer 'no' and leave. Good ones make the reader need to read more.

climax.text: 'Got Milk?' works because it creates a moment of self-check. You look at your fridge. That's the engagement.

punchline.text: Two words, one question mark. Milk sales saved.

quiz.question: What does Betteridge's Law state about question headlines?

details.summary: Question headlines engage the brain by creating an open loop that demands closure. Effective questions are ones the reader cannot answer without reading the content. details.whyItMatters: Questions transform passive scanning into active thinking. A well-crafted question headline turns the reader into a participant who must engage with the content to satisfy their curiosity.
takeaways: Questions create cognitive open loops that demand resolution
Headlines answerable with 'no' fail — the answer must be uncertain
Rhetorical questions engage less than genuinely surprising ones

faq.question: What is Betteridge's Law of Headlines?
faq.answer: Journalist Ian Betteridge observed that any headline written as a yes/no question can be answered 'no.' If readers can dismiss the question without reading, the headline fails. Effective question headlines require engagement with the content to find the answer.

faq.question: When do question headlines outperform statements?
faq.answer: When the question touches a genuine uncertainty the reader cares about. 'Are You Making This Common Resume Mistake?' works because the reader genuinely doesn't know. Questions targeting ego, fear, or curiosity consistently outperform generic informational questions.
